title: Fluid mechanics
note: Pressure grows with depth: p = p₀ + ρgh. For steady, incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline, Bernoulli's equation keeps p + ½ρv² + ρgh constant, so faster flow means lower pressure. The Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ compares inertial to viscous forces and predicts laminar or turbulent flow.

read.title: Speed, pressure, and drag
text: Fluids push on everything they touch. In a still liquid the pressure rises with depth, about one atmosphere for every 10 m of water, which is why dams are thicker at the bottom.

When a fluid moves, mass must be conserved. In a pipe that narrows, the same volume must pass every second, so the fluid speeds up. Bernoulli's equation then says its pressure falls, because for steady, frictionless, incompressible flow the sum of pressure, kinetic energy per volume, and potential energy per volume stays constant along a streamline. A Venturi meter uses that pressure drop to measure flow.

Real fluids are viscous. Right at a surface the fluid sticks, so a thin boundary layer forms where speed rises from zero. The Reynolds number, ρVL/μ, compares the inertia of the flow with its viscous forces. At low Reynolds number viscosity wins and the flow is smooth and laminar; at high Reynolds number it becomes turbulent.
Drag on a body follows D = ½ Cd ρ V² A, so doubling speed quadruples drag. Much of the drag on a blunt car comes from the wake behind it where flow separates, which is why streamlining helps so much.
